items.stem: Which of the following best describes "standing wave"?
options: A pipe with one end closed (a displacement node) and one end open (a displacement antinode)
A wave that transfers energy from one place to another through a medium or space
A wave pattern formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions, in which energy is not transferred along the wave
The frequency at which a system oscillates when displaced and released with no driving force
items.answer: A wave pattern formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions, in which energy is not transferred along the wave
items.markingKey: C. "standing wave" is a wave pattern formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions, in which energy is not transferred along the wave.

items.stem: Which property is the same for all points between two adjacent nodes?
options: displacement at each instant equal to the antinode
items.answer: phase
items.markingKey: A. All points in one loop oscillate in phase but with different amplitudes.

items.stem: Distinguish between a standing wave and a travelling wave.
items.answer: A standing wave has nodes and antinodes, amplitude that varies with position, all points between adjacent nodes in phase and no net energy transfer; a travelling wave has constant amplitude, phase that changes continuously along the wave and transfers energy.
items.markingKey: A standing wave has nodes and antinodes, amplitude that varies with position, all points between adjacent nodes in phase and no net energy transfer; a travelling wave has constant amplitude, phase that changes continuously along the wave and transfers energy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A string of length 0.90 m fixed at both ends vibrates with 5 loops. What is the wavelength?
A standing wave forms on a stretched cord in which waves travel at 24 m s⁻¹. The vibrator frequency is 30 Hz. Calculate the distance between adjacent nodes.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 0.800 m (M1); node spacing = λ/2 = 0.400 m (A1).

items.stem:
A microwave detector is moved away from a metal reflector. The position x of the n-th minimum (node) from a reference mark is recorded.

n / – | x / cm
1 | 3.40
2 | 4.86
3 | 6.24
4 | 7.70
5 | 9.14
6 | 10.62

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the wavelength of the microwaves. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State the wavelength with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) x (y) against n (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.44 cm; (c) 2.88 cm; (d) 2.88 cm ± 0.1 cm
items.markingKey: (a) x (y) against n (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 1.44 cm – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) λ = 2 × gradient = 2.88 cm (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 0.1 cm; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: What is the distance between two adjacent nodes in a standing wave of wavelength λ?
items.markingKey: B. Nodes are half a wavelength apart.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about formation of standing waves: nodes and antinodes is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Mohammed.)
options: In the steady state it vibrates at the driving frequency; it only vibrates at its natural frequency when this equals the driving frequency (resonance) or when free.
In a standing wave, the energy travels from one end to the other.
The wind was steady, not periodic; the collapse is better explained by aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting oscillation – a case where the textbook "resonance" story is an oversimplification.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength (λ/2) apart.
items.answer: In a standing wave, the energy travels from one end to the other.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: There is no net energy transfer along a standing wave; energy is stored in the oscillating loops.

items.stem: Explain how a standing wave is formed on a string fixed at both ends.
items.answer: A wave travels along the string and is reflected at the fixed ends; the incident and reflected waves have the same frequency, speed and (approximately) amplitude and travel in opposite directions, so they superpose to give fixed nodes and antinodes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A wave travels along the string and is reflected at the fixed ends; the incident and reflected waves have the same frequency, speed and (approximately) amplitude and travel in opposite directions, so they superpose to give fixed nodes and antinodes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Nodes are a wavelength apart." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength (λ/2) apart.
items.markingKey: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength (λ/2) apart. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "In a standing wave, the energy travels from one end to the other." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: There is no net energy transfer along a standing wave; energy is stored in the oscillating loops.
items.markingKey: There is no net energy transfer along a standing wave; energy is stored in the oscillating loops. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A string of length 1.2 m fixed at both ends vibrates with 3 loops. What is the wavelength?

A microwave detector is moved away from a metal reflector. The position x of the n-th minimum (node) from a reference mark is recorded.

n / – | x / cm
1 | 3.56
2 | 5.23
3 | 6.75
4 | 8.36
5 | 9.96
6 | 11.61

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the wavelength of the microwaves. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State the wavelength with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) x (y) against n (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.60 cm; (c) 3.20 cm; (d) 3.20 cm ± 0.1 cm
items.markingKey: (a) x (y) against n (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 1.60 cm – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) λ = 2 × gradient = 3.20 cm (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 0.1 cm; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: "Standing waves are simply travelling waves that have stopped moving." Discuss.
items.answer: Misleading: a standing wave is a superposition of two travelling waves; the medium oscillates, only the pattern is stationary.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the pattern does appear stationary; it is made of travelling waves. Arguments against: the medium still oscillates; only the pattern of nodes and antinodes is fixed; it results from superposition of two waves travelling in opposite directions; its properties (amplitude variation, phase relations, no energy transfer) differ fundamentally. Supported judgement: Misleading: a standing wave is a superposition of two travelling waves; the medium oscillates, only the pattern is stationary. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A student sets up microwaves (from a 10.5 GHz transmitter) reflecting off a metal plate and finds detector minima are not of zero intensity, becoming deeper closer to the plate. (a) Calculate the expected distance between minima. (b) Explain why the minima are not zero. (c) Explain why they are deeper near the plate.
items.answer: (a) λ = 2.86 cm, so minima 1.43 cm apart; (b) the reflected wave has smaller amplitude than the incident wave (spreading and absorption), so cancellation is incomplete; (c) near the plate the reflected wave has travelled less distance and spread less, so its amplitude is closer to the incident amplitude.
items.markingKey: λ = c/f = 2.86 cm (M1), spacing λ/2 = 1.43 cm (A1); unequal amplitudes (R1); reflected wave weakened by spreading/partial reflection (R1); amplitudes nearly equal close to the plate (R1).

items.stem: A string fixed at both ends has fundamental frequency f. What is the frequency of the third harmonic?
items.answer: 3f
items.markingKey: 3f (A1). All whole-number harmonics nf are possible on a string.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a guitar string sounds a higher note when it is pressed against a fret.
items.answer: Pressing at the fret shortens the vibrating length L; with the wave speed unchanged, the fundamental f = v/2L increases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pressing at the fret shortens the vibrating length L; with the wave speed unchanged, the fundamental f = v/2L increases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following statements about standing waves on strings and in pipes: harmonics is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Jonas.)
options: In the steady state it vibrates at the driving frequency; it only vibrates at its natural frequency when this equals the driving frequency (resonance) or when free.
Doubling the length of a string doubles its fundamental frequency.
There is no net energy transfer along a standing wave; energy is stored in the oscillating loops.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength (λ/2) apart.
items.answer: Doubling the length of a string doubles its fundamental frequency.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: f₁ = v/2L: doubling L halves the fundamental frequency.

items.stem: An organ pipe 1.1 m long is open at both ends; sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in the pipe. What is its fundamental frequency?
items.answer: 155 Hz
items.markingKey: A. Open pipe: f = v/2L = 155 Hz.

items.stem: What is the fundamental frequency of a pipe of length 0.34 m closed at one end? (speed of sound = 340 m s⁻¹)
items.answer: 250 Hz

items.stem: Hana writes: "A closed pipe can play its second harmonic at twice the fundamental frequency." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A closed pipe has no even harmonics; the next mode after the fundamental is at 3f₁.
items.markingKey: A closed pipe has no even harmonics; the next mode after the fundamental is at 3f₁. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a resonance-tube experiment a tuning fork of frequency 384 Hz is held over a tube whose closed end is a water surface. Loud resonances are heard at air-column lengths of 20.7 cm and 64.8 cm. (a) Show that the wavelength is 0.882 m. (b) Calculate the speed of sound. (c) Determine the end correction and explain why using two resonance lengths removes it.
items.markingKey: (a) L₁ + e = λ/4 and L₂ + e = 3λ/4 (M1), subtract: L₂ − L₁ = λ/2 (A1). (b) v = fλ = 339 m s⁻¹ (A1). (c) e = λ/4 − L₁ = 1.3 cm (A1); e cancels in the difference (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The resonance-tube method is an accurate way to measure the speed of sound in air."
items.answer: With successive resonances and repeat readings it can give v to within a few per cent – adequate, though less accurate than electronic time-of-flight methods.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: two successive resonance lengths remove the unknown end correction; simple, cheap apparatus; tuning forks have precise frequencies. Arguments against: judging the loudest point is subjective; end correction depends on tube diameter; temperature changes alter the speed during the experiment. Supported judgement: With successive resonances and repeat readings it can give v to within a few per cent – adequate, though less accurate than electronic time-of-flight methods. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "harmonic"?
options: A standing-wave mode whose frequency is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental frequency
Damping that returns a displaced system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating
Damping so large that the system returns slowly to equilibrium without oscillating
A point on a standing wave where the displacement is always zero
items.answer: A standing-wave mode whose frequency is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental frequency
items.markingKey: A. "harmonic" is a standing-wave mode whose frequency is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental frequency.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The lowest-frequency mode of standing wave that can be set up in a string or pipe"?
items.answer: fundamental (first harmonic)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of fundamental (first harmonic).

items.stem: A string vibrates in its third harmonic. How many nodes are there, including the ends?
items.markingKey: A. Three loops require four nodes.

items.stem: Outline how the data from an experiment testing L + e = v/(4f) for the first resonance of a closed tube, where e is the end correction should be linearised, and state the features of the graph that would confirm the relationship.
items.answer: Plot L (y-axis) against 1/f (x-axis); gradient = v/4. The y-intercept is −e, giving the end correction.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: L against 1/f (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = v/4 (A1). The y-intercept is −e, giving the end correction.

items.stem: Distinguish between the second harmonic of a string and the fundamental.
items.answer: The fundamental has one loop (L = λ/2); the second harmonic has two loops with a node at the centre (L = λ) and twice the frequency.
items.markingKey: The fundamental has one loop (L = λ/2); the second harmonic has two loops with a node at the centre (L = λ) and twice the frequency. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A pipe of length 0.60 m is closed at one end. The speed of sound is 343 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency of the fifth harmonic.
items.answer: 715 Hz
items.markingKey: Closed pipe: f = nv/4L with n odd (M1); f = 5 × 343/(4 × 0.60) = 715 Hz (A1).

items.stem: A pipe resonates at 220 Hz and next at 660 Hz, with no resonance in between. Deduce whether the pipe is open or closed at one end and calculate its length (speed of sound 336 m s⁻¹).
items.answer: closed at one end; L = 0.382 m
items.markingKey: ratio 660/220 = 3 → odd harmonics only, closed pipe (R1); λ₁ = 4L (M1); L = 0.382 m (A1).

items.stem: What is the fundamental frequency of a pipe of length 0.85 m closed at one end? (speed of sound = 340 m s⁻¹)
items.answer: 100 Hz

items.stem: In a resonance-tube experiment a tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz is held over a tube whose closed end is a water surface. Loud resonances are heard at air-column lengths of 15.4 cm and 48.7 cm. (a) Show that the wavelength is 0.666 m. (b) Calculate the speed of sound. (c) Determine the end correction and explain why using two resonance lengths removes it.
items.markingKey: (a) L₁ + e = λ/4 and L₂ + e = 3λ/4 (M1), subtract: L₂ − L₁ = λ/2 (A1). (b) v = fλ = 341 m s⁻¹ (A1). (c) e = λ/4 − L₁ = 1.3 cm (A1); e cancels in the difference (R1).

items.stem: Resonance occurs when
options: the amplitude of the driver is large
the driver is twice the natural frequency
the driving frequency equals the natural frequency
items.answer: the driving frequency equals the natural frequency
items.markingKey: D. Maximum energy transfer from driver to oscillator.

items.stem: In Barton’s pendulums, the paper-cone pendulum with the largest amplitude is the one that
options: has the same length as the driver pendulum
items.answer: has the same length as the driver pendulum
items.markingKey: B. Same length → same natural frequency → resonance.

items.stem: Distinguish between free oscillation and forced oscillation.
items.answer: A free oscillation occurs at the natural frequency after an initial displacement with no further input; a forced oscillation is maintained by a periodic driver and takes place at the driving frequency.
items.markingKey: A free oscillation occurs at the natural frequency after an initial displacement with no further input; a forced oscillation is maintained by a periodic driver and takes place at the driving frequency. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the London Millennium Bridge in 2000 as an example, explain resonance and positive feedback in forced oscillations.
items.answer: the bridge swayed sideways when crowds crossed on opening day; pedestrians adjusted their step to the sway, synchronising their footfalls The lateral natural frequency (~1 Hz) matched half the walking frequency and people locked into it, so the driving force grew; dampers were fitted to fix it
items.markingKey: Context (the bridge swayed sideways when crowds crossed on opening day; pedestrians adjusted their step to the sway, synchronising their footfalls) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the lateral natural frequency (~1 Hz) matched half the walking frequency and people locked into it, so the driving force grew; dampers were fitted to fix it – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to resonance and positive feedback in forced oscillations.

items.stem: A simple pendulum of length 0.60 m is pushed gently by a child once every cycle. Calculate the period of pushing that gives the largest amplitude (T = 2π√(l/g), g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.markingKey: Driving period = natural period (R1) = 2π√(0.60/9.81) = 1.55 s (A1).

items.stem: An aircraft wing has a natural frequency of 4.5 Hz. The engine propellers rotate at 2400 revolutions per minute with three blades. (a) Calculate the frequency at which blades pass the wing. (b) Explain whether resonance of the wing is likely at this rotation rate. (c) Explain what could happen during engine start-up as the propeller speed increases from zero.
items.answer: (a) 2400/60 × 3 = 120 Hz; (b) 120 Hz is far from 4.5 Hz, so the wing is not driven at resonance at cruise; (c) during start-up the blade-passing frequency passes through 4.5 Hz (at 90 rpm), so a brief large-amplitude vibration may occur; damping limits it.
items.markingKey: (a) 2400/60 × 3 = 120 Hz; (b) 120 Hz is far from 4.5 Hz, so the wing is not driven at resonance at cruise; (c) during start-up the blade-passing frequency passes through 4.5 Hz (at 90 rpm), so a brief large-amplitude vibration may occur; damping limits it.

items.stem: Define the term "forced oscillation".
items.answer: An oscillation of a system driven by a periodic external force at the driving frequency
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an oscillation of a system driven by a periodic external force at the driving frequency. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Lars is revising natural frequency, forced oscillations and resonance. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: In an open pipe there are nodes at both open ends.
A forced oscillator always vibrates at its natural frequency.
The wind was steady, not periodic; the collapse is better explained by aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting oscillation – a case where the textbook "resonance" story is an oversimplification.
Doubling the length of a string doubles its fundamental frequency.
items.answer: The wind was steady, not periodic; the collapse is better explained by aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting oscillation – a case where the textbook "resonance" story is an oversimplification.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. The wind was steady, not periodic; the collapse is better explained by aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting oscillation – a case where the textbook "resonance" story is an oversimplification.

items.stem: Explain how resonance is used in a microwave oven, and why the description "resonance of water molecules" is a simplification.
items.answer: Microwaves (2.45 GHz) drive polar water molecules to rotate, transferring energy that becomes internal energy; however 2.45 GHz is not a sharp natural frequency of water – the heating is broad dielectric absorption, so "resonance" is a simplification.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Microwaves (2.45 GHz) drive polar water molecules to rotate, transferring energy that becomes internal energy; however 2.45 GHz is not a sharp natural frequency of water – the heating is broad dielectric absorption, so "resonance" is a simplification. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Resonance means that the amplitude becomes infinite." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: With any damping the amplitude is finite; energy lost per cycle balances energy supplied.
items.markingKey: With any damping the amplitude is finite; energy lost per cycle balances energy supplied. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A 0.1 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 40 N m⁻¹ is driven by a variable-frequency vibrator. At which frequency is the amplitude largest?
items.markingKey: C. f₀ = (1/2π)√(k/m) = 3.18 Hz; resonance occurs here.

items.stem: A mass of 0.8 kg hangs from a spring of spring constant 60 N m⁻¹. The top of the spring is driven up and down by a vibration generator. Calculate the driving frequency at which resonance occurs. (f = (1/2π)√(k/m))
items.markingKey: Resonance at the natural frequency (R1); f₀ = (1/2π)√(60/0.8) = 1.38 Hz (A1).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed simply because the wind blew at its natural frequency." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The wind was steady, not periodic; the collapse is better explained by aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting oscillation – a case where the textbook "resonance" story is an oversimplification.
items.markingKey: The wind was steady, not periodic; the collapse is better explained by aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting oscillation – a case where the textbook "resonance" story is an oversimplification. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A tall building in a windy city has a natural sway frequency of 0.18 Hz. Engineers install a tuned mass damper (a large mass on springs near the top). (a) Explain what is meant by resonance in this context. (b) Explain why the damper must be tuned to 0.18 Hz. (c) Discuss one limitation of relying on a tuned mass damper.
items.answer: (a) Gusts or vortex shedding at about 0.18 Hz would drive the building at its natural frequency, giving large sway amplitude; (b) the damper oscillates out of phase with the building at that frequency, absorbing energy and reducing the amplitude; (c) it is effective only near its tuned frequency, the building’s frequency can change with loading or ageing, and it is heavy and expensive.
items.markingKey: Driving frequency = natural frequency → large amplitude (R1); periodic forcing source identified (A1); damper resonates in antiphase, transfers energy away and dissipates it (R1 R1); limitation with justification (R1).

items.stem: "Engineers should design structures with as much damping as possible." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Damping is valuable but must be balanced against cost; good design combines appropriate damping with natural frequencies away from expected driving frequencies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: damping limits resonant amplitude and fatigue; tuned mass dampers protect tall buildings in earthquakes and wind. Arguments against: damping adds cost, weight and maintenance; excessive damping can make structures stiff in other ways; shifting natural frequencies away from likely driving frequencies may be cheaper. Supported judgement: Damping is valuable but must be balanced against cost; good design combines appropriate damping with natural frequencies away from expected driving frequencies. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: With light damping, the peak of the resonance curve occurs at a frequency
items.answer: slightly below the natural frequency
items.markingKey: D. Damping shifts the peak slightly lower.

items.stem: Energy lost from a damped oscillator is mainly transferred to
options: internal (thermal) energy of the system and surroundings
items.answer: internal (thermal) energy of the system and surroundings
items.markingKey: A. Resistive forces dissipate energy.

items.stem: An oscillator of initial amplitude 20 mm loses 25 % of its amplitude each cycle. What is the amplitude after 3 cycles?
A student claims: "Critical damping means the system stops instantly." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without oscillating, not instantly.
items.markingKey: It returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without oscillating, not instantly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg sits on four springs, each of stiffness 3.0 × 10⁴ N m⁻¹. (a) Calculate the natural frequency of vertical oscillation, f = (1/2π)√(k_total/m). (b) The car drives over a washboard road with ridges 0.80 m apart; find the speed at which resonance occurs. (c) Explain why the shock absorbers are designed for near-critical damping.
items.answer: (a) k_total = 1.2 × 10⁵ N m⁻¹, f = (1/2π)√(1.2 × 10⁵/1200) = 1.59 Hz; (b) v = fλ = 1.59 × 0.80 = 1.27 m s⁻¹; (c) the body returns to equilibrium quickly after each bump without bouncing, improving comfort and keeping tyres in contact with the road.
items.markingKey: (a) k_total = 1.2 × 10⁵ N m⁻¹, f = (1/2π)√(1.2 × 10⁵/1200) = 1.59 Hz; (b) v = fλ = 1.59 × 0.80 = 1.27 m s⁻¹; (c) the body returns to equilibrium quickly after each bump without bouncing, improving comfort and keeping tyres in contact with the road.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The reduction in amplitude of an oscillation as energy is transferred out of the system by resistive forces"?
items.answer: damping
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of damping.

items.stem: Explain why critical damping is used in moving-coil meters and door closers.
items.answer: The pointer or door reaches its final position as quickly as possible without overshooting or oscillating, so it can be read (or closes) quickly and safely.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The pointer or door reaches its final position as quickly as possible without overshooting or oscillating, so it can be read (or closes) quickly and safely. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following statements about damping and its effects on resonance is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Zara.)
options: Open ends are displacement antinodes; the air there is free to move.
The amplitude varies from zero at nodes to a maximum at antinodes.
Damping changes the period of an oscillation dramatically.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength (λ/2) apart.
items.answer: Damping changes the period of an oscillation dramatically.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: Light damping hardly changes the period; it mainly reduces the amplitude over time.

items.stem: Jonas released a damped pendulum with a card sail and timed how long its amplitude took to fall to half its initial value. The 5 readings of the time for the amplitude to halve were 13.8, 13.6, 13.5, 13.0, 13.6 s. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 13.5 s (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.4 s (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.4/13.5 × 100 = 3.0 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: A lightly damped pendulum starts with amplitude 8.00 cm. Each oscillation the amplitude falls to 95 % of its previous value. Calculate the amplitude after 8 oscillations.

A student displaces a mass–spring system immersed in (i) air, (ii) water and (iii) thick syrup and records displacement against time. (a) Sketch and describe the three graphs. (b) Identify which might be close to critical damping and justify. (c) Explain, in terms of energy, why the amplitude in air decreases slowly.
items.answer: (a) Air: many oscillations, slowly decreasing amplitude (light damping); water: few oscillations quickly dying out; syrup: no oscillation, slow creep back to equilibrium (heavy damping). (b) Water could be near critical if it returns without overshoot in about a quarter-period; syrup is over-damped because it takes longer. (c) Air resistance removes only a small fraction of the energy each cycle, so the amplitude decays slowly and exponentially.
items.markingKey: Three correct descriptions (A1 A1); critical damping identified by fastest return without oscillation (R1); energy dissipated per cycle small in air (R1); link E ∝ A² (R1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "harmonic".
items.answer: A standing-wave mode whose frequency is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental frequency
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a standing-wave mode whose frequency is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental frequency. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A wave that transfers energy from one place to another through a medium or space"?
items.answer: travelling wave
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of travelling wave.

items.stem: Which is an example of useful resonance?
items.answer: Tuning a radio circuit to a station
items.markingKey: Tuning a radio circuit to a station (A1). Tuned circuits select one frequency by resonance.

items.stem: Distinguish between heavy damping and light damping.
items.answer: With light damping the system oscillates with slowly decreasing amplitude; with heavy damping it does not oscillate and returns to equilibrium slowly.
items.markingKey: With light damping the system oscillates with slowly decreasing amplitude; with heavy damping it does not oscillate and returns to equilibrium slowly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A closed pipe can play its second harmonic at twice the fundamental frequency." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A closed pipe has no even harmonics; the next mode after the fundamental is at 3f₁.
items.markingKey: A closed pipe has no even harmonics; the next mode after the fundamental is at 3f₁. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a standing wave does not transfer energy along the medium.
items.answer: The two component travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions; at nodes there is no motion, so no net energy passes along the medium – energy is stored, oscillating between kinetic and potential forms in each loop.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The two component travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions; at nodes there is no motion, so no net energy passes along the medium – energy is stored, oscillating between kinetic and potential forms in each loop. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Two identical pendulums hang from a horizontal string; a third, much longer pendulum is set swinging. What happens?
options: the long pendulum stops at once
the identical pendulums swing with large amplitude at their natural frequency
the two identical pendulums oscillate with small amplitude at the frequency of the long pendulum
items.answer: the two identical pendulums oscillate with small amplitude at the frequency of the long pendulum
items.markingKey: D. Off-resonance forced oscillations are small and at the driving frequency (Barton’s pendulums).

items.stem: Two resonance curves are drawn for the same oscillator with different damping. The more heavily damped curve has
options: a peak at a much higher frequency
items.answer: a lower, broader peak
items.markingKey: A. More damping → lower and broader.

items.stem: Priya and a classmate in Melbourne disagree about standing waves on strings and in pipes: harmonics. Which statement is correct?
options: A closed pipe has no even harmonics; the next mode after the fundamental is at 3f₁.
Resonance means that the amplitude becomes infinite.
Doubling the length of a string doubles its fundamental frequency.
Critical damping means the system stops instantly.
items.answer: A closed pipe has no even harmonics; the next mode after the fundamental is at 3f₁.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. A closed pipe has no even harmonics; the next mode after the fundamental is at 3f₁.

items.stem: A standing wave forms on a stretched cord in which waves travel at 60 m s⁻¹. The vibrator frequency is 20 Hz. Calculate the distance between adjacent nodes.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 3.00 m (M1); node spacing = λ/2 = 1.50 m (A1).

items.stem: With reference to MRI scanners in hospitals, explain how it illustrates resonance as selective energy absorption.
items.answer: protons in a strong magnetic field absorb radio waves strongly only at the Larmor frequency Energy is absorbed only when the driving (radio) frequency equals the natural precession frequency
items.markingKey: Context (protons in a strong magnetic field absorb radio waves strongly only at the Larmor frequency) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: energy is absorbed only when the driving (radio) frequency equals the natural precession frequency – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to resonance as selective energy absorption.

items.stem: Amara filmed a mass–spring system oscillating in water and measured the halving time of the amplitude from the video. The 5 readings of the time for the amplitude to halve were 9.9, 9.9, 9.9, 10.2, 10.1 s. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 10.0 s (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.1 s (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.1/10.0 × 100 = 1.5 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: Waves travel at 180 m s⁻¹ on a 0.65 m string fixed at both ends. What is the frequency of harmonic 4?
items.answer: 554 Hz
items.markingKey: D. f = nv/2L = 554 Hz.

items.stem: A microwave detector moved along the line between a transmitter and a metal plate passes through 7 consecutive minima over a distance of 8.40 cm. Calculate the wavelength and frequency of the microwaves.
items.markingKey: 7 minima = 6 node spacings of λ/2 (M1); λ = 2 × 8.40/6 = 2.80 cm (A1); f = c/λ = 1.07 × 10¹⁰ Hz (A1).

items.stem: A simple pendulum of length 1.5 m is pushed gently by a child once every cycle. Calculate the period of pushing that gives the largest amplitude (T = 2π√(l/g), g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.markingKey: Driving period = natural period (R1) = 2π√(1.5/9.81) = 2.46 s (A1).

items.stem: An oscillator of initial amplitude 20 mm loses 10 % of its amplitude each cycle. What is the amplitude after 2 cycles?
Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The resonance-tube method is an accurate way to measure the speed of sound in air."
items.answer: With successive resonances and repeat readings it can give v to within a few per cent – adequate, though less accurate than electronic time-of-flight methods.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: two successive resonance lengths remove the unknown end correction; simple, cheap apparatus; tuning forks have precise frequencies. Arguments against: judging the loudest point is subjective; end correction depends on tube diameter; temperature changes alter the speed during the experiment. Supported judgement: With successive resonances and repeat readings it can give v to within a few per cent – adequate, though less accurate than electronic time-of-flight methods.

items.stem: "Standing waves are simply travelling waves that have stopped moving." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Misleading: a standing wave is a superposition of two travelling waves; the medium oscillates, only the pattern is stationary.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the pattern does appear stationary; it is made of travelling waves. Arguments against: the medium still oscillates; only the pattern of nodes and antinodes is fixed; it results from superposition of two waves travelling in opposite directions; its properties (amplitude variation, phase relations, no energy transfer) differ fundamentally. Supported judgement: Misleading: a standing wave is a superposition of two travelling waves; the medium oscillates, only the pattern is stationary. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Engineers should design structures with as much damping as possible."
items.answer: Damping is valuable but must be balanced against cost; good design combines appropriate damping with natural frequencies away from expected driving frequencies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: damping limits resonant amplitude and fatigue; tuned mass dampers protect tall buildings in earthquakes and wind. Arguments against: damping adds cost, weight and maintenance; excessive damping can make structures stiff in other ways; shifting natural frequencies away from likely driving frequencies may be cheaper. Supported judgement: Damping is valuable but must be balanced against cost; good design combines appropriate damping with natural frequencies away from expected driving frequencies. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "Critical damping is always the best choice for any oscillating system." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Critical damping suits systems that must settle quickly; others, such as instruments and resonators, need light damping.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fastest return without overshoot for meters, suspensions and doors. Arguments against: musical instruments and clocks need light damping to oscillate; earthquake isolation may need different behaviour; heavy damping may be safer where any overshoot is dangerous. Supported judgement: Critical damping suits systems that must settle quickly; others, such as instruments and resonators, need light damping. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A pipe closed at one end has length L. What is the wavelength of its fundamental?
items.answer: 4L
items.markingKey: C. A node at the closed end and antinode at the open end: L = λ/4.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "antinode".
items.answer: A point on a standing wave where the amplitude of oscillation is a maximum
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a point on a standing wave where the amplitude of oscillation is a maximum. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The large increase in amplitude that occurs when the driving frequency equals (or is close to) the natural frequency of the system"?
items.answer: resonance
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of resonance.

items.stem: Lukas and a classmate in Seoul disagree about damping and its effects on resonance. Which statement is correct?
options: Doubling the length of a string doubles its fundamental frequency.
A closed pipe can play its second harmonic at twice the fundamental frequency.
It returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without oscillating, not instantly.
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed simply because the wind blew at its natural frequency.
items.answer: It returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without oscillating, not instantly.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. It returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without oscillating, not instantly.

items.stem: The air temperature in a closed organ pipe increases. Which change occurs to the fundamental?
options: its wavelength increases and frequency is unchanged
its frequency increases and its wavelength is unchanged
items.answer: its frequency increases and its wavelength is unchanged
items.markingKey: D. λ is fixed by L; v increases so f increases.

items.stem: A standing wave can be formed with which pair of waves?
options: two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions
a transverse and a longitudinal wave
two waves of equal frequency in the same direction
two waves of different frequency in the same direction
items.answer: two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions
items.markingKey: A. Opposite directions and the same frequency are essential.

items.stem: Explain why a washing machine shakes violently at one particular spin speed during spin-up.
items.answer: As the drum speeds up the driving frequency passes through the natural frequency of the machine on its mounts; at that speed resonance gives large amplitude, which decreases again as the frequency increases further.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: As the drum speeds up the driving frequency passes through the natural frequency of the machine on its mounts; at that speed resonance gives large amplitude, which decreases again as the frequency increases further. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between light damping and heavy damping.
items.answer: With light damping the system oscillates with slowly decreasing amplitude; with heavy damping it does not oscillate and returns to equilibrium slowly.
items.markingKey: With light damping the system oscillates with slowly decreasing amplitude; with heavy damping it does not oscillate and returns to equilibrium slowly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline how the data from an experiment testing f = v/(2L) for the fundamental of a string of variable length L should be linearised, and state the features of the graph that would confirm the relationship.
items.answer: Plot f (y-axis) against 1/L (x-axis); gradient = v/2 (half the wave speed). A straight line through the origin confirms f ∝ 1/L.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: f against 1/L (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = v/2 (half the wave speed) (A1). A straight line through the origin confirms f ∝ 1/L.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "In a standing wave, the energy travels from one end to the other." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: There is no net energy transfer along a standing wave; energy is stored in the oscillating loops.
items.markingKey: There is no net energy transfer along a standing wave; energy is stored in the oscillating loops. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the quartz crystal in a watch, explain how it illustrates useful resonance.
items.answer: a quartz crystal is driven electrically and oscillates at its sharp natural frequency of 32 768 Hz The crystal responds strongly only at its natural frequency, giving a very stable reference for timekeeping
items.markingKey: Context (a quartz crystal is driven electrically and oscillates at its sharp natural frequency of 32 768 Hz) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the crystal responds strongly only at its natural frequency, giving a very stable reference for timekeeping – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to useful resonance.

items.stem: The amplitude of a damped mass–spring system decreases by a factor of 0.9 every cycle. Determine the fraction of the original energy that remains after 8 cycles.

The first resonance length L of a tube closed at one end is measured for tuning forks of different frequency f. Theory: L = v/(4f) − e, where e is the end correction.

f / Hz | L / cm
256 | 33.0
288 | 29.3
320 | 26.4
384 | 21.8
426.7 | 19.5
512 | 16.1

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the speed of sound in air. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State the speed of sound with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) L in m (y) against 1/f in s (x); (b) gradient ≈ 86.7 m s; (c) 347 m s⁻¹; (d) 347 m s⁻¹ ± 7 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) L in m (y) against 1/f in s (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 86.7 m s – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) v = 4 × gradient = 347 m s⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 7 m s⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem:
A microwave detector is moved away from a metal reflector. The position x of the n-th minimum (node) from a reference mark is recorded.

n / – | x / cm
1 | 3.55
2 | 5.18
3 | 6.77
4 | 8.38
5 | 9.93

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the wavelength of the microwaves. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State the wavelength with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) x (y) against n (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.60 cm; (c) 3.19 cm; (d) 3.19 cm ± 0.2 cm
items.markingKey: (a) x (y) against n (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 1.60 cm – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) λ = 2 × gradient = 3.19 cm (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 5 % of the value = 0.2 cm; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: With reference to the London Millennium Bridge in 2000, explain how it illustrates resonance and positive feedback in forced oscillations.
items.answer: the bridge swayed sideways when crowds crossed on opening day; pedestrians adjusted their step to the sway, synchronising their footfalls The lateral natural frequency (~1 Hz) matched half the walking frequency and people locked into it, so the driving force grew; dampers were fitted to fix it
items.markingKey: Context (the bridge swayed sideways when crowds crossed on opening day; pedestrians adjusted their step to the sway, synchronising their footfalls) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the lateral natural frequency (~1 Hz) matched half the walking frequency and people locked into it, so the driving force grew; dampers were fitted to fix it – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to resonance and positive feedback in forced oscillations.

items.stem: "Critical damping means the system stops instantly." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without oscillating, not instantly.
items.markingKey: It returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without oscillating, not instantly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a resonance-tube experiment a tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz is held over a tube whose closed end is a water surface. Loud resonances are heard at air-column lengths of 15.5 cm and 48.6 cm. (a) Show that the wavelength is 0.662 m. (b) Calculate the speed of sound. (c) Determine the end correction and explain why using two resonance lengths removes it.
items.markingKey: (a) L₁ + e = λ/4 and L₂ + e = 3λ/4 (M1), subtract: L₂ − L₁ = λ/2 (A1). (b) v = fλ = 339 m s⁻¹ (A1). (c) e = λ/4 − L₁ = 1.1 cm (A1); e cancels in the difference (R1).

items.stem: "A tuned mass damper is simply a form of critical damping." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: No: a tuned mass damper uses resonance of a secondary system plus damping; it is not the same as critical damping.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: both reduce the amplitude of unwanted oscillations. Arguments against: a tuned mass damper is a second oscillator resonating in antiphase that transfers energy away; critical damping refers to the decay of free oscillations without overshoot; dampers are effective only near the tuned frequency. Supported judgement: No: a tuned mass damper uses resonance of a secondary system plus damping; it is not the same as critical damping. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
